slides.0.title: VQA and Labelling
slides.0.subtitle: Provincial VQA, percentage rules, icewine rules and Cellared in Canada
slides.1.title: What VQA is
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Provincial management
slides.1.highlights.0.content: VQA is the Vintners Quality Alliance; Ontario and BC have stricter provincial rules, including 100% local grapes. Wines must pass laboratory and panel testing to carry the VQA seal (The Canadian Encyclopedia)
slides.1.highlights.1.title: Ontario
slides.1.highlights.1.content: VQA Ontario was incorporated in 1998 and now operates as the Ontario Wine Appellation Authority; the legal base is the Vintners Quality Alliance Act, 1999, proclaimed on 29 June 2000 (Wine With Seth)
slides.1.highlights.2.title: British Columbia
slides.1.highlights.2.content: In August 2005 the province took over the system with the Wines of Marked Quality Regulation (B.C. Reg. 79/2005), creating the BC VQA appellation of origin, enforced by the BC Wine Authority; that regulation was repealed by B.C. Reg. 168/2018 on 27 July 2018 (BC VQA website, BC Laws)
slides.1.content: There is no single national VQA law: each province runs its own.
slides.2.title: Percentage rules
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Ontario's three tiers
slides.2.highlights.0.content: VQA Ontario: 100% Ontario grapes; a regional appellation (such as Niagara Peninsula): more than 85% from that region, with up to 15% from elsewhere in Ontario; a sub-appellation: 100% from that sub-appellation. The geographical indication must appear on the front label (VQA Ontario)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Vintage and variety
slides.2.highlights.1.content: Ontario: a vintage may appear if 85% or more of the grapes come from one vintage; categories such as icewine, botrytized and late harvest wines must show a vintage. As a general principle, declarations must be supported by at least 85% content (VQA Ontario)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: BC's percentages
slides.2.highlights.2.content: BC VQA requires 100% BC grapes; under the current regulation (B.C. Reg. 168/2018) a GI other than "British Columbia" needs at least 85% of the grapes from that GI's area, with the rest from elsewhere in BC; the vintage needs at least 85% and a single-varietal name at least 85% of the wine by volume (BC Laws). An earlier source (Wine With Seth) gave 95%; the current regulation is followed here
slides.2.content: Both provinces use 85% for vintage and variety; for place, Ontario's sub-appellations need 100% and BC's GIs 85%.
slides.3.title: Icewine and Cellared in Canada
slides.3.highlights.0.title: Ontario icewine
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Grapes must freeze naturally on the vine and be harvested below -8°C, with juice of at least 35°Brix; Late Harvest needs at least 22, Select Late Harvest 26 and Special Select Late Harvest 30°Brix. Icewine must be 100% icewine, with the viticultural area on the front label (VQA Ontario)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: BC icewine
slides.3.highlights.1.content: Varieties are limited to Vitis vinifera or Vidal Blanc; grapes freeze naturally on the vine at -8°C or lower and are pressed frozen; must reaches at least 32°Brix after each pressing and averages at least 35°Brix in the vessel; residual sugar at bottling is at least 100 g/L. Icewine and Meritage are restricted to the BC VQA programme (Wine With Seth)
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Cellared in Canada
slides.3.highlights.2.content: A category of wine blended from imported bulk wine and Canadian wine. BC allows 100% foreign content; Ontario allows no more than 60% foreign content and no dilution with water; from 1 April 2014 Ontario wineries existing before 1993 may make "International - Canadian" blends with up to 75% foreign content. VQA wines, by contrast, are 100% Canadian grapes (Wikipedia)
slides.3.content: Only VQA means 100% Canadian grapes; Cellared in Canada does not.
